analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover telemental health on equal terms with in-person care.
analysis.headline: The bill gained 22 cosponsors from both parties but died in three House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill says that when a health plan covers mental health or substance use care, it must cover care delivered by video or phone the same way it covers care delivered in an office — same limits, same costs, same rules. Existing law already requires insurers to treat mental health benefits comparably to medical benefits; this bill writes that rule explicitly for telehealth, which became a main channel for mental health care during the pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private health insurance who use teletherapy or telepsychiatry, especially in rural areas and for substance use treatment, where telehealth is often the only practical option. It stops insurers from charging more or imposing tighter limits on virtual mental health visits than on office visits.

how_it_helps.text: It applies existing mental health parity rules to telehealth benefits in exactly the same way they apply to in-person benefits, so plans cannot impose different cost-sharing, visit limits, or prior-authorization rules on virtual mental health care [S2][S3].

The bill reaches group health plans and individual coverage through the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the tax code — the same three statutes that carry current parity law — so it covers most privately insured Americans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employers would bear whatever added claims come from expanded use of virtual mental health care, and premiums could rise modestly. Some costs could also pass to patients through premiums rather than per-visit charges.

drawbacks.text: Mandating equal coverage of telehealth could raise premiums if it increases the volume of covered visits, a cost employers and enrollees would share [S3].

Parity rules on paper have historically been underenforced; the bill states the requirement but adds no new auditing or penalty provisions, so patients may still need to file complaints to get equal treatment [S2][S3].
Equal coverage does not guarantee access: it does not require plans to have enough telemental health providers in network, nor does it help the uninsured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward and targeted: closing a gap that would let insurers treat video and phone therapy as second-class care. The main costs are modest premium pressure and weak enforcement teeth, which an honest supporter would acknowledge. The bill is a clarification of an existing principle rather than a new program, so its upside and downside are both limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Manning introduced the bill on June 24, 2022, joined by Reps. Doris Matsui and Brian Fitzpatrick — a Democrat, a Democrat, and a Republican [S1][S3].
It was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — meaning any one of them had to act for it to move [S1][S5].
The committees took no further action, and the bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or Senate consideration before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
It attracted 22 cosponsors, 21 Democrats and 1 Republican, showing some bipartisan appetite that was never tested with a vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep the ability to impose stricter limits and cost-sharing on virtual mental health care than on in-person care, without a statutory rule closing that gap. Patients who rely on teletherapy gain nothing; they pay out of pocket or forgo care at the same rate as before.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 21 Democrats and 1 Republican of 22 cosponsors — and the record shows no partisan opposition, only inaction: no committee or chamber ever voted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill removes insurers' ability to treat virtual mental health visits differently from office visits — higher copays, visit caps, or extra authorization. Their interest in keeping that flexibility runs against patients who need teletherapy.

Equal coverage makes telehealth a first-class benefit, sustaining demand for virtual therapy and psychiatric care after pandemic-era rules expire. Better reimbursement prospects also help patients get care.
